title: CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out
goal: By the end you can recover from a failure at the right stage, unwrap CompletionException, give each call its own timeout, and ask several suppliers at once without one bad answer failing the whole request.
opening:
Last lesson, an order moved through the kitchen like a tray from station to station, and each station was a stage of a `CompletableFuture`. Nobody stood by the grill waiting.

Now the steak burns. The grill cook can't pass it on as if nothing happened, and the sauce cook has no business pouring sauce on charcoal. So the tray carries a note: "burned at the grill". Every later station passes it along untouched, until someone at the pass, the counter where dishes leave the kitchen, reads the note and decides what table 4 gets.

`CompletableFuture` handles failure the same way, with three surprises. The note sometimes arrives in an envelope. A timer that tells the manager to stop waiting doesn't stop the cook. And waiting for three dishes at once fails the whole table when one of them burns. All three pass a quick test, because tests rarely burn the steak.

In this lesson, we'll follow a failure down a pipeline, open the envelope and put deadlines on slow calls. Then we'll ask three suppliers for a price without letting one bad answer spoil the rest. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A pipeline reads `supplyAsync(this::grill, kitchen).thenApply(this::addSauce).thenApply(this::plate).exceptionally(ex -> apology)`. `grill` throws an `IllegalStateException`. What happens?
options: `addSauce` and `plate` run with a null steak
`addSauce` and `plate` are skipped, and `exceptionally` gets the exception wrapped in a `CompletionException`
`supplyAsync` throws the exception on the calling thread
`addSauce` and `plate` are skipped, and `exceptionally` gets the `IllegalStateException` itself
warmup.why: A failed stage skips every later `thenApply` until a handler. The handler gets a `CompletionException` with the `IllegalStateException` as its cause, because the exception was thrown inside a stage. The last option is the tempting one, and code that checks `ex instanceof IllegalStateException` there is quietly wrong. The first two sections show both halves.

sections.h: A dish burns at the grill: how a failure skips every step until a handler
sections.body:
Let's put the kitchen into code. A **stage** is one step attached to a future, such as a `thenApply`, that runs when the step before it has finished. Our grill runs on a pool called `kitchen`, and three plain stages follow it, one per station. Then come two handlers, which we'll meet in a moment:

```java
CompletableFuture<String> result = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(ErrorPathDemo::grill, kitchen)
        .thenApply(s -> step("1. pour the sauce on " + s, s + " with pepper sauce"))
        .thenApply(s -> step("2. plate " + s, "a plate of " + s))
        .thenApply(s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got " + s))
        .whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("whenComplete sees: " + (ex == null ? v : ex)))
        .exceptionally(ex -> {                              // the pass
            System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex);
            return "table 4 got an apology and the menu";
        });
```

```kotlin
val result = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(::grill, kitchen)
    .thenApply { s -> step("1. pour the sauce on $s", "$s with pepper sauce") }
    .thenApply { s -> step("2. plate $s", "a plate of $s") }
    .thenApply { s -> step("3. carry it to table 4", "table 4 got $s") }
    .whenComplete { v, ex -> println("whenComplete sees: ${ex ?: v}") }
    .exceptionally { ex ->                                  // the pass
        println("exceptionally sees: $ex")
        "table 4 got an apology and the menu"
    }
```

`step` prints its text and returns the value, so we can see which stations did any work. And `grill` always throws an `IllegalStateException` that says `the steak burned`. Before you read on, decide which numbered lines will print.

`ErrorPathDemo`, in the Try it below, printed this:

```text
whenComplete sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned
exceptionally sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned
result: table 4 got an apology and the menu
```

Not one numbered line. When a stage throws, its future **completes exceptionally**: it finishes with an exception instead of a value. Every `thenApply`, `thenCompose` and `thenCombine` after it is then skipped. Its function never runs, and its own future fails with the same cause. That's the note on the tray, passed from station to station.

The failure stops at the first **handler**, a stage that also runs when the step before it failed. There are four:

| Method | Runs on | Changes the outcome? |
|---|---|---|
| `exceptionally(ex -> value)` | failure only | yes, replaces the failure with a value |
| `handle((value, ex) -> result)` | success and failure | yes, returns any result |
| `whenComplete((value, ex) -> ...)` | success and failure | no, passes the outcome on |
| `exceptionallyCompose(ex -> future)` | failure only | yes, with another future (JDK 12) |

`whenComplete` is the manager who glances at every tray on its way past and writes in the log. It sees both outcomes and hands the same one on, so it suits logs and counters. (One detail: if its own action throws after a success, the result becomes that new failure. After a failure, the original failure wins.) `exceptionally` is the pass. It replaces the failure with a value, and everything after it sees a success.

Where you put the handler decides what you can still save. At the end, after the sauce, the plate and the walk to table 4 were all skipped, the only honest thing left is an apology. Move the handler up, right after the grill, and it can swap in a spare steak. Then every station after it works as if nothing had gone wrong. Run the demo with `early`, and it prints:

```text
exceptionally sees: java.util.concurrent.CompletionException: java.lang.IllegalStateException: the steak burned
1. pour the sauce on the spare steak
2. plate the spare steak with pepper sauce
3. carry it to table 4
whenComplete sees: table 4 got a plate of the spare steak with pepper sauce
```

**Recover as close to the failure as you can. Every step after the handler then runs as usual.**

Sometimes the fallback takes time of its own. Cooking a new steak on the second grill returns a future, not a steak. For that case, use `exceptionallyCompose`. It is to `exceptionally` what `thenCompose` is to `thenApply`:

```java
CompletableFuture<String> steak = grill.cookAsync(order)
        .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> spareGrill.cookAsync(order));   // JDK 12+: the fallback is a future too
```

```kotlin
val steak: CompletableFuture<String> = grill.cookAsync(order)
    .exceptionallyCompose { spareGrill.cookAsync(order) }          // JDK 12+: the fallback is a future too
```

Look again at what our two handlers printed, though. They didn't get our `IllegalStateException`. They got a `CompletionException` with ours inside, like a note sealed in an envelope. Where did the envelope come from?

sections.h: The note in an envelope: when a handler gets CompletionException, and when it doesn't
sections.body:
Handlers don't always get your exception. They get one of two things, by a rule that surprises everyone once.

A **`CompletionException`** is an unchecked exception that `CompletableFuture` wraps around a failure, with your exception inside as its cause. It's the envelope.

If the exception was thrown inside a stage, by a `supplyAsync` task or a `thenApply` function, the future stores it in an envelope. A handler on that future, or on any later stage, gets the `CompletionException`, and `getCause()` returns your exception. That's what our burned steak did.

If somebody completed the future by hand, with `completeExceptionally(ex)`, the future stores `ex` just as it is. `orTimeout`, which the next section covers, works that way, and so do many libraries that hand you a future. A handler attached right to that future gets the bare exception. One stage later it's in an envelope again, because the failure crossed a stage boundary on its way.

`WrapDemo` prints every case. Cover the output below, and predict each line before you read it:

```text
1. handle() on the supplyAsync future      CompletionException <- IllegalStateException
2. handle() on completeExceptionally       IllegalStateException
3. handle() one stage later                CompletionException <- IllegalStateException
4. handle() after orTimeout                TimeoutException
5. get() throws                            ExecutionException <- IllegalStateException
6. join() throws                           CompletionException <- IllegalStateException
```

Lines 2 and 4 are bare, because someone completed those futures by hand. The last two lines are the blocking calls from the last lesson: `get()` throws `ExecutionException` and `join()` throws `CompletionException`, both with the original exception as the cause.

So a handler that checks `ex instanceof TimeoutException` can be right in one place and quietly wrong one stage further down. Open the envelope first, then decide:

```java
.exceptionally(ex -> {
    Throwable cause = (ex instanceof CompletionException && ex.getCause() != null) ? ex.getCause() : ex;
    if (cause instanceof TimeoutException) return lastWeeksPrice;
    throw new CompletionException(cause);       // not ours to handle: keep failing
})
```

```kotlin
.exceptionally { ex ->
    val cause = if (ex is CompletionException && ex.cause != null) ex.cause!! else ex
    if (cause is TimeoutException) lastWeeksPrice
    else throw CompletionException(cause)       // not ours to handle: keep failing
}
```

First we take the cause out, if there is an envelope. Then we handle the one case we know, a timeout, with last week's price. The last line reads as "I opened it, and this one isn't mine, so pass it on." Throwing inside a handler keeps the future failing, so a later handler, or the caller, can deal with it.

The lab's `unwrap` method does the same job in a loop. It also strips the `ExecutionException` that `get()` adds, in case one wrapper ends up inside another. And on a future you know has failed, `exceptionNow()` (JDK 19) hands you the exception with the envelope already removed.

**Open the envelope before you test the type. Rethrow what isn't yours.**

Line 4 of the demo came from a timeout. A timeout looks like the cure for a slow call. It is only half of one.

sections.h: A kitchen timer for the manager: orTimeout ends the wait, not the work
sections.body:
Timeouts need a scene of their own. The restaurant buys flour from a few suppliers, and each supplier has a **web service**: a program on another computer that answers questions over the network. Ask it for today's price of a sack of flour, and it answers within a few hundred milliseconds. On a bad day, it doesn't answer at all.

In code, asking is a blocking call. It holds a thread until the answer comes, just like the slow web service from Sizing a pool. So picture the call as a cook on the phone to the supplier. The manager wants the price, so he starts a kitchen timer. When it rings, he stops waiting and decides without it. Nobody tells the cook, who stays on hold, listening to the supplier's music.

JDK 9 gave `CompletableFuture` two such kitchen timers:

```java
price.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);                       // fails with TimeoutException
price.completeOnTimeout(lastWeeksPrice, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);  // completes with a default
```

```kotlin
price.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                        // fails with TimeoutException
price.completeOnTimeout(lastWeeksPrice, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)   // completes with a default
```

Both change the future you call them on, and return it. If the future hasn't completed when the time is up, a timer thread inside the JDK completes it: `orTimeout` with a `TimeoutException`, `completeOnTimeout` with the value you gave it. The thread's name depends on the JDK. On JDK 21 it's `CompletableFutureDelayScheduler`, and on JDK 25 it's `ForkJoinPool.commonPool-delayScheduler`. Plain stages attached to the future then run on that thread, so keep them cheap.

Now the trap. Neither timer touches the call. `KeepsRunningDemo` gives a 600 ms call to a slow supplier a deadline of 200 ms. On JDK 21 it printed this:

```text
  36 ms  io-1                                   asking the slow supplier for a price
 236 ms  CompletableFutureDelayScheduler        the future completed with TimeoutException
 695 ms  io-1                                   the supplier answered, but nobody is listening
 702 ms  main                                   pool closed
```

The future failed right on time. The call finished anyway, about 600 ms after it started, holding `io-1` the whole way, and `close()` had to wait for it. The answer went nowhere.

Maybe `cancel(true)` can hang up the phone? Run the demo with `cancel`:

```text
 243 ms  main                                   cancel(true) returned true
 247 ms  main                                   the future completed with CancellationException
 773 ms  io-1                                   the supplier answered, but nobody is listening
```

As far as the future knows, the cancel worked. The line `interrupted: the call stops here` never printed, though, so the call never noticed. The `CompletableFuture` Javadoc says the flag `mayInterruptIfRunning` "has no effect in this implementation because interrupts are not used to control processing."

The source code shows why. `supplyAsync` hands the pool a small task that points to the future. The future keeps no pointer back to that task, or to the thread that runs it. So `cancel` can only store a `CancellationException` as the result. There's no thread it could interrupt.

The `FutureTask` that `submit` returns is the opposite. Its `cancel(true)` sends an interrupt, the polite request to stop from Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption.

Here the kitchen picture breaks. A real manager could walk over and tell the cook to hang up. A `CompletableFuture` has no line back to its cook at all.

Under load, that is how a pool fills up with nothing. Take a pool of 20 threads and a supplier that hangs for 30 seconds. Every request gets its `TimeoutException` after 300 ms, right on time. But every call holds its thread for 30 seconds. After 20 requests, all 20 cooks are on hold. New calls, even to healthy suppliers, wait in the pool's queue behind them and time out too.

So every call to another computer needs two timeouts. The one on the future is the caller's deadline. The one inside the client, such as the request timeout of Java's HTTP client, makes the call itself give up, and that gives the thread back:

```java
HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri)
        .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))    // the call itself gives up after 300 ms
        .build();
```

```kotlin
val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri)
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))        // the call itself gives up after 300 ms
    .build()
```

Set the client's timeout no longer than the future's. And give each supplier a limit of its own, a bulkhead from Sizing a pool, so one hung supplier can't take every thread.

**A timeout on the future frees the caller, not the thread. Give the call its own timeout too.**

One call with a deadline is under control now. But the manager doesn't want one price. He wants three, and he wants them at the same time.

aside.title: Does a framework's timeout stop the work?
aside.body: If you write web services, your framework or a fault-tolerance library may let you put a timeout on a method with an annotation, often called `@Timeout`. Ask it the same question as `orTimeout`: when the time is up, does only the wait end, or does the work stop too? Some tools run the method on another thread and simply stop waiting for it. Others also interrupt that thread, which stops the call only if the call responds to interrupts. Either way, the client's own timeout is what reliably gives the thread back.

With `cancel`, `cancel(true)` returns `true` and the future completes with `CancellationException` on `main`, but the line `interrupted` never prints: the call runs to the end.

sections.h: Three suppliers at once: allOf, anyOf, and one bad answer that mustn't spoil the rest
sections.body:
Back to the flour. Three suppliers sell it: the corner shop, the market and the mill. The manager wants today's price from all three, and he'll buy from the cheapest. Phoning them one after another wastes time, so three cooks phone at once. Sending out several calls at the same time and collecting the answers is called a **fan-out**. In code, it's three futures, all started before we wait for any of them.

`FanOutDemo` sets up the three suppliers with delays chosen for teaching. The corner shop fails after 50 ms, because it's closed today. The market answers 21.50 after 100 ms, and the mill answers 19.80 after 300 ms. The JDK has two methods that combine many futures, and the demo tries both.

`allOf(f1, f2, f3)` returns a `CompletableFuture<Void>` that completes when all three have completed. It carries no results of its own. You read them from your own futures with `join()`, which no longer blocks, because they're all done. Predict what `-Pargs=all` prints, then compare:

```text
  84 ms  corner fails
 151 ms  market answers 21.50
 333 ms  mill answers 19.80
 336 ms  all: failed with java.lang.IllegalStateException: corner is closed today
```

Two good prices came back, and the errand failed anyway. If any of its futures fails, `allOf` fails too, and only after the slowest one has finished. (Every timestamp runs a little late, because the clock starts before the pool does, and the machine was busy with other work.)

`anyOf(f1, f2, f3)` returns a future that completes the same way as the first of them to finish. Here's `-Pargs=any`:

```text
  99 ms  corner fails
 161 ms  any: failed with java.lang.IllegalStateException: corner is closed today
 161 ms  market answers 21.50
 352 ms  mill answers 19.80
```

The corner shop answered first, with the worst possible news, and `anyOf` took it. The first to finish includes failures. If you want the first *successful* answer, `anyOf` can't give it to you. (Go deeper has a ten-line helper for that.)

So neither method does the errand on its own. The fix is to make each call unable to fail before we combine them. Give every call its own deadline, then turn any failure into "no answer":

```java
CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> safe = ask(supplier)
        .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                       // this supplier's deadline
        .handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.empty());
```

```kotlin
val safe: CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> = ask(supplier)
    .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                          // this supplier's deadline
    .handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() }
```

`handle` sees both outcomes and returns a new result either way: the price inside an `Optional`, or an empty `Optional`. Now `allOf` over the safe futures can only succeed, and the step after it picks the lowest price that came back. Here's `-Pargs=safe`:

```text
  91 ms  corner fails
 170 ms  market answers 21.50
 340 ms  mill answers 19.80
 353 ms  safe: result 19.80
```

That's the mill's price, the cheapest, from the slowest supplier. The closed corner shop turned into an empty `Optional`, and it spoiled nothing.

The deadline must sit on each call. Put one `orTimeout` on the `allOf` instead, and a single hung supplier throws away the two good answers along with its own silence.

**Make each call unable to fail before you combine them. Then pick from what came back.**

That's the lab. Its `QuoteAggregator` asks every supplier for a quote, a price offer, all at the same time. Each call gets its own deadline, every skipped supplier is reported with its real cause, and the lowest price wins.

Notice the limit of the tool before we leave the phones. A `CompletableFuture` is good at waiting for calls and combining their answers. It can't stop a call it gave up on, and when one call fails, it doesn't cancel the others. It was built for work that waits. For work that is all arithmetic, the JDK has a pool of its own.

compare.title: One supplier call with a deadline: CompletableFuture vs coroutines

java.title: Ask.java (CompletableFuture)

kotlin.title: Ask.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)

compare.note: Both versions have the same shape: a deadline, then a failure turned into "no answer". The difference is what happens to the work. `orTimeout` only completes the future, and the supplier call runs to its end. Kotlin's coroutines, its own light tasks with a track of their own, can do more. `withTimeoutOrNull` cancels the block when time is up, and `runInterruptible` turns that cancellation into `Thread.interrupt()` on the IO thread. So a blocking call that responds to interrupts stops and gives its thread back. In both languages, a call that ignores interrupts keeps its thread, which is why the client's own timeout still matters. Kotlin has one trap of its own: when you catch `Exception`, you must rethrow `CancellationException` by hand, or the coroutine stops responding to cancellation. `CompletableFuture` has no such trap.

worked.title: Give the flour price a deadline and a fallback

steps.say: The kitchen gets the flour price from its main supplier through an async client, a library whose methods return a `CompletableFuture`. When the supplier hangs, everything that needs the price hangs with it. Before reading on, decide what should happen after 300 ms.
steps.alt_code:
fun price(item: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> =
    supplier.priceAsync(item)             // no deadline: a hung supplier hangs the kitchen

steps.say: Give the call a deadline, count failures without changing them, then fall back to a second supplier, which has an async client too. `metrics` is a small counter that a dashboard reads. The fallback gets a short deadline of its own, because `exceptionallyCompose` starts a new call that the first timeout doesn't cover.

Why `unwrap` in the counter? The supplier's client may complete its future with a bare exception, `orTimeout` stores a bare `TimeoutException`, and anything thrown inside a stage arrives in an envelope. Without unwrapping, half the failures would be counted as `CompletionException`, which tells the person reading the dashboard nothing.

One gap is left. After 300 ms the kitchen moves on, but the main call still holds a thread and a network connection. Give the request a timeout of its own, so the client gives up too. With the JDK's HTTP client, it's one line on the request.
steps.alt_code:
val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri)
    .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300))        // 5. the call stops waiting too
    .build()

lab.title: A price checker that survives bad suppliers
steps: Meet the classes. A `QuoteProvider` is one supplier's price service: `quote(item)` makes a blocking call and returns today's price, or throws. A `Quote` is one answer, the supplier's name and its price. `QuoteAggregator.best(item)` must ask every supplier at once and complete with the lowest `Quote`. Its Javadoc is the spec. Run the tests: all seven fail.
Write `unwrap`: loop while the throwable is a `CompletionException` or an `ExecutionException` and has a cause, moving to the cause each time.

Add a private method `ask(QuoteProvider p, String item)` that returns `CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>>`: `supplyAsync` on `io`, then `orTimeout`, then `handle`. On failure, call `onSkip.accept(p.name(), unwrap(ex))` and return `Optional.empty()`.

In `best`, map every supplier to `ask`, collect the futures in a list, and pass them to `allOf`. In the `thenApply` after it, `join` each future, keep the quotes that are present, and return the lowest price, or throw `NoQuoteException`.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then once more.
hints: `orTimeout` takes a `long` and a unit: `orTimeout(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)`.
`allOf` takes an array (`asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)`) and returns `CompletableFuture<Void>`. Read the quotes from your own list.

If `skipsFailingProvider` reports a `CompletionException`, you passed `ex` to `onSkip` without unwrapping it. If `skipsSlowProvider` times out, the deadline is on the whole call, not on each supplier.
Throwing `NoQuoteException` inside the `thenApply` is enough: the returned future fails with it as the cause.

drill.title: A price with a deadline and a fallback
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> price(String item)`: call `main.priceAsync(item)` with a 300 ms deadline. If it fails for any reason, log the unwrapped cause and fall back to `backup.priceAsync(item)`, which returns a `CompletableFuture` too. Then compare. Which method did you use for the fallback, and did you unwrap before logging?

answer.title: Prices.java

alt.title: Prices.kt
alt.src:
fun price(item: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> =
    main.priceAsync(item)
        .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .exceptionallyCompose { ex ->
            val cause = if (ex is CompletionException && ex.cause != null) ex.cause!! else ex
            log.warn("main supplier failed, asking the backup: {}", cause.toString())
            backup.priceAsync(item)                  // a future, so exceptionallyCompose, not exceptionally
        }

recap: A failure skips every later stage until a handler. `exceptionally` and `handle` can recover, `whenComplete` only looks, and `exceptionallyCompose` (JDK 12) recovers with another future.
Recover as close to the failure as you can, so that every stage after the handler runs as usual.
An exception thrown inside a stage reaches handlers wrapped in a `CompletionException`. `completeExceptionally` and `orTimeout` store it bare. Unwrap before you test the type.
`orTimeout` and `completeOnTimeout` end the caller's wait, not the work, and `cancel(true)` on a `CompletableFuture` interrupts nothing. Give the call its own timeout in the client.

`allOf` waits for every future and fails if any failed. `anyOf` takes the first to finish, failures included. For a fan-out, give each call its own deadline and turn its failure into "no answer" before `allOf`.
The limit: a `CompletableFuture` can stop waiting but can't stop the work, and one failed call doesn't cancel the others. It suits work that waits, not one big pile of arithmetic.
closing:
We started with a steak that burned at the grill. Its note skipped every station on the way to the pass, sometimes in an envelope. The kitchen timer freed the manager while the cook stayed on hold. And three suppliers gave one price, once no call could spoil the errand.

Now search your own code for `orTimeout(`, and check that the call underneath has a timeout of its own. Then search for `allOf(`, and make sure every future it waits for has its own deadline and handler.

Next, we'll go back to the chopping board, where the work is all arithmetic. How does a `ForkJoinPool` keep every cook busy on one big job, with no manager handing out tickets?

quiz.q: Each step prints its letter: `supplyAsync(fails, io).thenApply(A).whenComplete(B).exceptionally(C).thenAccept(D)`, and the supplier throws. What prints?
options: B and C, then the pipeline fails
quiz.why: `A` is skipped, because its input failed. `whenComplete` runs on a failure too, but it passes the failure on, so `C` runs and recovers. Then `D` runs with the fallback value. After `exceptionally` recovers, every stage after it sees a success, which is why the last option is wrong.

quiz.q: `supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("closed today"); }, io).exceptionally(ex -> ...)`. What is the class of `ex`?
quiz.why: The exception was thrown inside a stage, so the future stores it wrapped in a `CompletionException`. `ExecutionException` is what `get()` throws at the blocking edge. You would get the bare `IllegalStateException` only if someone had called `completeExceptionally` with it.

quiz.q: Supplier calls run on a fixed pool of 20 threads with `orTimeout(300, MILLISECONDS)`. One supplier hangs for 30 s, and 100 requests arrive in one second. What happens?
options: The first 20 time out at 300 ms but keep their threads; later calls queue behind them, so they time out too, even to healthy suppliers
Every request times out at 300 ms, and the pool stays free
`orTimeout` interrupts the hung calls, so the threads come back at 300 ms
quiz.why: `orTimeout` completes the future but never touches the call, so each hung call holds its thread for 30 s. A fixed pool has a queue with no limit, so nothing is rejected: new calls just wait behind the hung ones until their own deadlines pass. A timeout in the client and a limit per supplier prevent it.

quiz.q: You want to count every supplier call as a success or a failure, without changing what the caller receives. Which method fits?
quiz.why: `whenComplete` sees both outcomes and passes the original one on. `handle` sees both too, but you'd have to rebuild the outcome yourself, rethrowing the failure, which is easy to get wrong. `exceptionally` misses successes, and `thenAccept` misses failures.

quiz.q: From "Callable, Future, cancellation and interruption": the same blocking call, asleep in `Thread.sleep`, runs twice: once through `executor.submit(task)` and once through `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, executor)`. You call `cancel(true)` on both futures. What happens?
options: Only the `submit` call is interrupted; the `CompletableFuture` one keeps sleeping
Neither, because `cancel` only affects tasks that haven't started
quiz.why: `submit` returns a `FutureTask`, whose `cancel(true)` interrupts the worker thread. `CompletableFuture.cancel` ignores the flag: it completes the future with `CancellationException` and leaves the task alone. Both futures report `isCancelled() == true`.

flashcards.front: Which CompletableFuture handler sees a failure but can't change the outcome?
flashcards.back: `whenComplete`. It passes the original result or failure on. `exceptionally` and `handle` can replace it.

flashcards.front: A handler on a failed `supplyAsync` future: which exception does it get?
flashcards.back: A `CompletionException`, with the exception the task threw as `getCause()`.
No. It completes the future with `TimeoutException`, and the task keeps running, holding its thread.
No. The flag has no effect. The future completes with `CancellationException`, and the task runs on.

flashcards.front: One of three futures fails at 50 ms, and the slowest takes 300 ms. When does `allOf` complete?
flashcards.back: At 300 ms, exceptionally. `allOf` waits for all of them; it doesn't fail fast.

flashcards.front: What does `anyOf` give you if the fastest future fails?
flashcards.back: A failure. `anyOf` completes like the first future to complete, success or failure.

flashcards.front: When do you use `exceptionallyCompose` instead of `exceptionally`?
flashcards.back: When the fallback is itself a future, such as a call to a backup supplier (JDK 12+).

terms.plain: One step attached to a future, such as a thenApply, that runs when the step before it finishes.
The unchecked wrapper CompletableFuture puts around an exception thrown inside a stage.
Runs only on failure and replaces it with a value.
Runs on success or failure and returns a new result either way.
Runs on success or failure to look; passes the outcome on unchanged.
Fails the future with TimeoutException if it isn't done in time. The work keeps running.
Sending several calls at the same time and collecting their answers.
Combine many futures: wait for all of them, or take the first to complete.

explain_back.prompt: A friend's price checker does `allOf(askCorner, askMarket, askMill).orTimeout(500, MILLISECONDS)` and then picks the lowest price. Explain why it fails whenever one supplier is closed or slow, and how you would change it.
explain_back.answer: `allOf` fails if any of its futures fails, so one closed supplier fails the whole call, and only after the slowest supplier has finished. The single `orTimeout` on the `allOf` means one hung supplier makes the whole call time out and throws away the prices that did come back. I'd give each supplier call its own `orTimeout`, then a `handle` that turns a failure into an empty `Optional` and reports the unwrapped cause. Then `allOf` over those safe futures can't fail, and the step after it picks the lowest price among the ones that are present, or fails with a clear "no quote" error if all are empty. I'd also set a timeout in the HTTP client, because `orTimeout` doesn't stop the call itself.
